title: Checkpoint: A Universe of Galaxies
objective: After this level you can describe the universe’s structure from our galaxy up to the cosmic web.
summary: From the Milky Way to the Local Group, clusters and the cosmic web: a universe of galaxies, all moving apart.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale. Zoom out as far as galaxies go.
cards.body: Start at home, with the Sun circling the Milky Way. Then keep zooming: our neighborhood, cities of galaxies, and the biggest pattern in the universe.

cards.headline: A ladder of scale
cards.body: Climb it one rung at a time. The Sun circles the Milky Way once every 230 million years or so. The Milky Way is one of about 100 or more galaxies in the Local Group, our small town. Bigger still are clusters of hundreds or thousands of galaxies, cities held together largely by dark matter. And we're not at the top yet.

cards.headline: The cosmic web
cards.body: At the top of the ladder, galaxies and clusters form a vast web of long filaments and sheets wrapped around huge, nearly empty voids. Picture the foam in a bubble bath: galaxies in the soapy film, emptiness in the bubbles. And the whole web is stretching as the universe expands, which is why distant galaxies look redshifted. The largest pattern in the universe is still stretching.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: Galaxies are spiral, elliptical or irregular
Local Group → clusters → the cosmic web
Dark matter holds galaxies and clusters together

questions.prompt: On the largest scales, how are galaxies arranged?

options.label: Spread perfectly evenly through space
In one giant sphere around the Milky Way
options.rationale: The Milky Way isn’t at any center.

options.label: In a web of filaments and sheets around voids
In a single flat disk, like one huge spiral
options.rationale: The structure is a web, not a disk.

questions.explanation: Galaxies and clusters form a cosmic web of filaments and sheets surrounding vast, nearly empty voids.

questions.prompt: Which list runs from smallest to largest?

options.label: Milky Way, Local Group, galaxy cluster, cosmic web
Local Group, Milky Way, cosmic web, galaxy cluster
options.rationale: The Milky Way is one member of the Local Group.

options.label: Galaxy cluster, Milky Way, Local Group, cosmic web
options.rationale: A cluster holds hundreds or thousands of galaxies.

options.label: Cosmic web, galaxy cluster, Local Group, Milky Way
options.rationale: That runs from largest to smallest.

questions.explanation: Our galaxy belongs to the Local Group; bigger clusters hold hundreds or thousands of galaxies; clusters are strung along the cosmic web.

questions.prompt: A galaxy’s outer stars orbit much faster than its visible matter can explain. What is the most likely reason?

options.label: A quasar is pushing its outer stars
options.rationale: Quasars don’t speed up outer stars.

options.label: Unseen dark matter is adding gravity
It is colliding with Andromeda
options.rationale: A collision wouldn’t explain this pattern.

options.label: Redshift makes the stars look fast
options.rationale: Redshift reveals distance, not orbital speed.

questions.explanation: Stars moving too fast for the visible mass were the key evidence for dark matter.

questions.prompt: A faraway galaxy shows a very large redshift. What does that tell you?

options.label: It is made mostly of red giant stars
It is heading toward the Milky Way
options.rationale: Approaching light would shift toward blue.

options.label: It is an elliptical full of old stars
options.rationale: Shape can’t be read from redshift.

options.label: It is very far away and receding fast

questions.explanation: A big redshift means a distant galaxy, carried away quickly by the expansion of space.

questions.prompt: Chapter 9 recap: why can a galaxy cluster act as a gravitational lens?

options.label: Its hot gas works like a glass lens
options.rationale: The bending comes from gravity, not gas.

options.label: Its quasars focus light into beams
options.rationale: Quasars don’t focus other galaxies’ light.

options.label: Its enormous mass bends passing light
Its galaxies reflect light toward us

questions.explanation: A cluster’s huge mass, much of it dark matter, bends and magnifies the light of galaxies behind it.
